messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 52, Ramesh Patel had been working for years as a housecleaner in a downtown hotel, moving quietly through guest rooms with his cart, changing linens, scrubbing bathrooms, and trying to leave each room looking untouched. Divorced and living alone in a small apartment, he had taken pride in being dependable, careful, and respectful in other people’s spaces. The event that now organized so much of his inner life happened on an ordinary workday, which made it harder for him to set it apart from the rest of his days. He had been cleaning a bathroom when another worker entered the room behind him. In the cramped space, with the floor still slick and supplies out, something he did in those few seconds led to the other person being seriously injured. When he tells it, he does not tell it as a flowing story. He sees it as separate images: the wet tile catching the light, the other worker’s body losing balance, the sound of impact, the position in which the man landed. Each image arrives sharply, as if cut out from time, and he can picture them with painful clarity.

What stays with Ramesh is not only fear but a fierce, immediate rage that flares when the memory returns. In session he is startled by how quickly it comes over him. He can be speaking quietly and then feel heat in his chest, his jaw tightening, his hands clenching. The anger is difficult for him to explain, except that the whole thing feels intolerable and he cannot bear that those moments happened exactly as they did. He does not describe himself as an angry man in general; what torments him is that the memory itself comes charged, and when it does he is back inside those pictures with the same force.

Since the injury, the world around him has seemed full of traps for remembrance. The return of the memory is often instantaneous and without warning. At work, the shine of freshly mopped bathroom tile, the sight of a cleaning cart parked at a doorway, or the small choreography of stepping aside in a tight room can bring back the full scene before he has time to prepare himself. A moment earlier he is folding towels; the next he is seeing the tile, the fall, the aftermath. Because he works in the same kind of environment in which the accident occurred, he encounters these moments repeatedly. He has found himself hesitating before entering bathrooms, waiting in hallways until he is sure no one else is nearby, taking longer routes so he does not have to pass coworkers in narrow spaces. These habits have slowed him down, and supervisors have noticed that rooms take him longer than they used to. He feels humiliated by that too, because being efficient and careful had always been part of how he understood himself.

Over the months after the accident, Ramesh had come to believe that what happened revealed something unforgivable about him. He speaks about the injury not as a terrible mistake but as proof that he acted in a way that violated his own character. He is certain the event happened because of the way he acted, and he returns again and again to what he should have done differently in those few seconds. In his mind there is no neutral version of the story; there is only that he failed to be the kind of person he believed himself to be. For a man who had long valued being conscientious and harmless, this has become a painful moral injury. He says, with a flatness that is more striking than tears, that he does not know what his life stands for now. Nothing feels meaningful anymore. He still goes to work, pays his bills, comes home, reheats food, and sleeps fitfully, but these activities feel emptied out. The structure of life remains while its point has fallen away.

His divorce predates the accident, and he lives without much daily companionship. Since the injury he has become even more inward, not because he has offered elaborate explanations to others, but because he cannot imagine saying aloud the thing that most preoccupies him: that he did this, and that it says something final about him. In the hotel he keeps conversations brief. He avoids joking with coworkers the way he once did, in part because even ordinary contact near housekeeping tasks can make him abruptly tense and bring those snapshots back. The result is a more isolated workday and a lonelier evening when the same images can surface again.

What brought Ramesh to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but the accumulation of these moments until they seemed to occupy every part of the day. He became frightened by how completely a small detail in his surroundings could seize him, and by how little he could feel about his future besides blame and emptiness. Sitting in treatment now, he says he wants some way to live without being ambushed by those pictures. What frightens him most is not only remembering the accident but the possibility that he is right about what it means—that one act has defined him permanently, and that nothing in his life will feel worthwhile again.
